lead: 224 decision support tools for metal additive manufacturing, scored on whether each accounts for four costs and four benefits of adopting it. Select one or more column cards to filter; select a row to read the rating notes, the tool link and sources.
foot: Scope: commercial software, academic models, government and consortium tools, and methods or standards, published 2010 onward, all metal AM processes, with a defense sustainment lens. Ratings reflect public documentation as of October 2026. No means a full description of the tool was read, or its documented scope plainly excludes the item; Unknown means the public evidence is too thin to tell, which is common for internal government tools and products described only in press releases. Where a tool was released more than once, only the newest release is listed and earlier ones are named under What it is. Polymer-only cases whose methods transfer to metal are kept and flagged.

tools.name: NIAR Additive Manufacturing Techno-Economic Analysis cost model and TEA module (America Makes IMPACT project 5554.007)
tools.developer: Wichita State University National Institute for Aviation Research (NIAR), VALDOS group (team listed in the briefing: Brady Williams, R. Andrulonis, M. Shaw, L. Tubesing, C. Combemale, P. Funk; no PI is labeled). Funded by OSD ManTech through AFRL agreement FA8650-20-2-5700 and administered by America Makes (project 5554.007; IMPACT Topic 8, Project 2).
tools.year: 2023–2025 (period of performance Nov 14, 2023 to May 14, 2025; no final deliverable found publicly as of Oct 2026)
tools.context: DoD-wide, not Air Force-only. It targets sourcing gaps where castings and forgings are hard to get. Advisory board: Army DEVCOM AvMC, NAVSEA, AFLCMC (the only Air Force member, Beth Dittmer), DLA R&D, NASA, Boeing, GE Additive, BAE Systems and America Makes. No Air Logistics Complex or RSO member is listed.
tools.processes: L-PBF, laser/electron-beam DED, wire-arc AM, additive friction stir deposition (AFSD)
tools.availability: Deliverables go to America Makes and DoD: a 4-modality cost model with a TEA module, a value-proposition framework, a manufacturing readiness report and a manuscript. No public release, final report or newer description was found.
tools.description: A cost model for four metal AM modalities, plus a techno-economic analysis (TEA) module 'to be used by DoD personnel to aid in the decision of when to leverage AM'. The stated objective is to 'deliver a framework for when, where, and how to utilize metal AM technologies to bridge gaps in component sourcing.' The team compared 13 existing cost models and used advisory-board and government interviews to find omitted cost elements; the stated future work is to 'implement the gaps into a tool.' This update re-read the Jan 2024 interim briefing and searched for other NIAR tools built for the Air Force. None were found. NIAR's other Air Force work is B-1/F-16 digital twins, WAM materials data and scanning/reverse engineering. The ratings describe the planned cost structure in the interim briefing, not a verified final tool.

NRE.note: The interim briefing lists 'NRE (DFAM, engineering salary, etc.)' only as an item in an 'Initial Gap Analysis for LPBF Cost Model' (slide 13), and CAD/DFAM/machine-setup rows appear in a literature-review table of cost elements by modality. The NIAR/TEA model is a planned deliverable with no values, formulas or calculations published.

Production.note: Per-modality cost elements (feedstock, build plate, machine cost, depreciation, labor, energy, gas, build time, post-processing) are listed from a review of 13 existing cost models. NIAR's own model is planned ('implementation of gaps into deliverable tool'), and no calculation or values are public.

QA_Qual.note: Appears only as 'supplier learning curve/common qualification', an industry-maturation factor. There is no qualification-campaign cost element (interim briefing).

QA_Insp.note: 'Quality Control' appears as a row in the literature-review cost-element table, and 'inspection rate per part application' appears as a gap item for a planned LPBF model. No inspection-cost method or values are public.

Storage.note: The advisory board flagged 'Packaging and storage' as an element missing from traditional cost models, to be added in the TEA module. It is not shown as quantified.

Shared_Capital.note: Machine depreciation, wrap rates and the build-plate packing factor spread capital within builds. No sharing across a part portfolio or across users is shown.

Shared_Capacity.note: The interim briefing's objective says 'when, where, and how' but has no site, location, capacity or utilization content, and the final tool is not public.

Speed.note: 'Readiness/AOG', 'costs associated with inoperable equipment and/or vehicles' and 'supply chain alleviation' are listed as TEA factors to add. Lead time is not modeled in the briefing.

tools.name: DLA Legacy Parts AM Prescreening Tool (DLA prototype AM candidate selection tool)
tools.developer: LMI with XSB Inc., Penn State (T. Simpson) and Virginia Tech (C. Williams), for the Defense Logistics Agency Weapon System Sustainment Program
tools.context: DLA-managed Class IX legacy spare parts (all services)
tools.processes: All metal and polymer AM (matched against the Senvol machine/material database)
tools.availability: Government internal prototype; method published in LMI report DL501T1 (DTIC)
tools.description: A database query tool that narrows about 4.5 million DLA-managed parts to about 43,000 that fit an AM build envelope and exactly match a common AM feedstock, assuming no redesign. Users then filter by FSC, weapon system, criticality, lead time, unit cost, dimensions, material and machine, with engineering review of each candidate's technical data package (TDP) required before any decision.

NRE.note: TDP availability is a displayed attribute, a proxy for reverse-engineering need; NRE is not costed and no redesign is assumed.

Production.note: Unit cost (current price) is a filter; no AM production cost is computed.

QA_Qual.note: Criticality codes are a filter in the prototype; first-article testing and QA-plan requirements are discussed as considerations, not tool fields. No burden estimate.

QA_Insp.note: Production lot testing (with FAT and QAP) is listed in Chapter 2 of the LMI report only as a general consideration for engineers. It is not among the nine logistics attributes, the prototype filters or display, or the proposed data elements (LMI DL501T1, Ch. 3-4).

Storage.note: Annual demand and backorder status are proposed data elements; stock on hand is only a consideration. No inventory or holding-cost analysis.

Shared_Capital.note: Not addressed.

Shared_Capacity.note: Not addressed.

Speed.note: Combined administrative plus production lead time and backorder data are filters; not converted to readiness value.

tools.name: NAVSEA AM part risk triage and TDP approval framework (with NAMPIE part identification events)
tools.developer: Naval Sea Systems Command (NAVSEA 05T, AM Technical Warrant Holder)
tools.context: US Navy surface ships and submarines; shipboard and waterfront AM

tools.description: Parts are sorted into color-coded risk boxes: Yellow (under triage), Green (low criticality; can be approved at the waterfront or aboard ship), Blue (requires NAVSEA HQ review) and Red (cannot or should not be made by AM). NAMPIE events identify candidate shipboard parts, and a 'buy or print' Mission Impact Analysis uses the NAVSUP Price Fighter cost tool.

QA_Qual.note: Criticality category sets the approval level (waterfront vs NAVSEA HQ vs prohibited), a qualitative proxy for qualification burden.

QA_Insp.note: Only a public briefing describes the framework, and it does not mention inspection or NDE in the triage.

Storage.note: The briefing mentions only digital file storage and does not say whether physical inventory is considered in triage.

Shared_Capital.note: The briefing does not mention equipment cost, and the framework's internal criteria are not public.

Shared_Capacity.note: The briefing mentions a digital manufacturing enclave to 'facilitate distributed manufacturing' but does not say whether triage considers capacity across ships or sites.

Speed.note: The briefing cites readiness through 'production of obsolete or long-lead items' as a program goal but does not say whether lead time enters the triage.

tools.name: CASTOR (CASTOR Enterprise / automatic part identification)
tools.developer: Castor Technologies Ltd. (described as Israeli in earlier coverage; Fabbaloo 2021 calls it California-based); resold by Siemens (CASTOR Enterprise; Teamcenter-X & CASTOR), integrated into Oqton MOS (Apr 2023), listed on Hexagon Nexus
tools.year: 2020 (earliest coverage); Light/Enterprise/White Label editions by Jun 2021; 2D-drawing analysis Jul 2022; Oqton MOS integration Apr 2023; Siemens Xcelerator Nov 2023; used in NSRP Navy shipbuilding project May 2023-May 2024
tools.context: US Navy submarine sustainment: the NSRP project '3D Printing of Supply Sensitive Parts' (GD NASSCO per NSRP page; NAVSEA and PEO SSBN sponsors; GD Electric Boat observer) used CASTOR to screen Ohio-, Los Angeles- and Virginia-class parts by NIIN. Also general industry (Stanley Black & Decker, Evonik); Siemens lists aerospace & defense and marine among target industries.
tools.processes: Metal and polymer AM with a configurable printer/material library. Metal printers used in the NSRP run: SLM 280 2.0, EOS M400-4, Concept Laser M2 cusing Multilaser, X160Pro (likely ExOne X1 160Pro binder jet; not stated in deck). Metal materials: 316L, 304L, 17-4PH, IN625, IN718, Invar 36, CuNi2SiCr, AlSi10Mg. Polymer: HP Jet Fusion 4200 (PA11/PA12).
tools.availability: Commercial license (enterprise SaaS, cloud or internal server; free trial Jan 2024; Light, Enterprise and White Label editions; Siemens Xcelerator / Teamcenter-X; Oqton MOS integration)
tools.description: Bulk-screens 3D CAD, 2D PDF drawings, BOMs or part metadata spreadsheets. For each part it flags printability (printable / printable with changes / unprintable, with reasons such as threads, metal-support milling, heat deformation and wall thickness) and picks a printer and material. It then estimates AM cost and conventional-manufacturing cost in dollars, plus AM lead time in days. Other outputs: break-even versus CNC and die casting, redesign options (cheapest, best match, weight reduction, consolidation), FEA and CO2. Enterprise adds printer ROI calculations and a customizable calculation structure.

NRE.note: Flags 'printable with changes', grades metal-support removal difficulty by simulated CNC milling, extracts 2D PDF drawings into 3D representations and suggests redesigns; none of this effort is costed (NSRP deck 2024; Fabbaloo 2021; 3DPrint.com 2022).

Production.note: Per-part AM cost vs traditional-manufacturing cost in dollars on named metal printers (e.g., check valve AM $368.98 vs TM $868.17) (NSRP deck 2024).

QA_Qual.note: The NSRP deck and marketing show only technical screens and no qualification field, but the Enterprise edition's customizable calculation structure is not public, so qualification costing cannot be ruled out.

QA_Insp.note: No source read, including the NSRP output tables, mentions inspection, and the full cost model is not public.

Storage.note: Marketed for 'digital warehouses' and legacy MRO spares, framed as digital inventory vs stocked spares; no holding-cost or inventory model documented (Siemens Teamcenter-X & CASTOR page; 3DPrint.com 2022; Fabbaloo 2021).

Shared_Capital.note: Enterprise edition includes 'ROI calculations for 3D printers' and users can enter in-house printers, but amortization/utilization inputs are not documented (3D ADEPT 2021; NSRP deck 2024). Earlier pass rated No.

Shared_Capacity.note: Public sources show in-house printer settings and a link to service bureaus but no capacity model, and full product documentation is not public.

Speed.note: Produces AM lead-time estimates and time savings; lead-time reduction is an acceptance criterion (not dollarized into readiness).

tools.name: Rickenbacher integrated SLM cost model
tools.developer: L. Rickenbacher, A. Spierings, K. Wegener (ETH Zurich / inspire AG)
tools.context: Industrial SLM job-shop costing; parts from different projects pooled into mixed build jobs
tools.processes: L-PBF (SLM)
tools.availability: Published model (Rapid Prototyping Journal 19(3):208-214); equations in paper, no public software
tools.description: Adapts Alexander et al.'s generic cost model to SLM, covering pre- and post-processing steps plus a regression-based build-time estimate for mixed build jobs. It allocates build cost to parts by volume and build height so that parts of different size and complexity sharing one build each get a fair cost. Building parts simultaneously gave a 41% average cost reduction in the case study.

NRE.note: Geometry-data preparation and build-job assembly are cost elements (per Dogea et al. 2023's description of the model). These are recurring build prep, with no redesign, reverse engineering or parameter development.

Production.note: Core output is total cost per part for parts of differing size, complexity and quantity; each process step is modelled (Emerald abstract).

QA_Qual.note: Only the abstract and two secondary descriptions were read; Dogea et al. (2023) say nothing about quality or qualification, so whether the model includes them is not established.

QA_Insp.note: The abstract says the model covers all pre- and post-processing steps, but neither it nor the secondary descriptions say whether inspection is one of them (only heat treatment and HIP are confirmed absent).

Storage.note: Outside the documented scope: the model allocates SLM process-step costs to parts in shared build jobs, which does not involve inventory (Emerald abstract).

Shared_Capital.note: Explicitly models simultaneous builds of multiple parts from different projects, with cost-allocation algorithms; 41% average per-part reduction (abstract). Rudolph & Emmelmann 2018 describe the split by volume and build height.

Shared_Capacity.note: Pooling happens only within one machine's build jobs, as a cost effect; no lead-time or multi-site capacity effect.

Speed.note: Not addressed.

tools.name: Lindemann et al. (2013) DMRC lifecycle-cost model with TD-ABC
tools.developer: C. Lindemann, U. Jahnke, M. Moi, R. Koch (Paderborn University, Direct Manufacturing Research Center)
tools.context: Lifecycle cost of AM vs. conventional manufacturing for end-use parts (wheel carrier, Formula Student upright); aerospace/automotive framing
tools.processes: L-PBF (SLM/DMLS)
tools.availability: Published model (SFF Symposium 2012 and 2013 papers); no public software
tools.description: Lifecycle cost model following the DIN/IEC 60300-3-3 phases: concept, design and development, production, installation, usage/maintenance, and disposal. Production is costed with time-driven activity-based costing across build-job preparation, build, part and support removal, and post-processing. Build rate, machine cost, material cost and utilization come out as the dominant drivers.

NRE.note: The design and development phase is costed explicitly: component design, QM planning, prototyping and testing, and production planning. Build-job preparation is also costed. The optimized redesign breaks even at about 250-425 pieces (SFF 2013).

Production.note: TD-ABC of machine, material, personnel, energy, consumables and post-processing, with complexity factors per build job (SFF 2013).

QA_Qual.note: QM planning and prototyping/testing appear as design-phase lifecycle costs, but no material/process qualification or certification burden is modelled (SFF 2013).

QA_Insp.note: Quality control is listed among the TD-ABC production cost elements; no NDI/CT or coupon-testing detail seen (SFF 2013).

Storage.note: The usage/maintenance phase includes logistics support with spare-part storage, but the on-demand inventory benefit of AM is not modelled (SFF 2013).

Shared_Capital.note: TD-ABC allocates machine cost by resource time and names utilisation among the most critical cost factors, though utilisation is a single 75% assumption (about 673 parts/yr) that is never varied (SFF 2013).

Shared_Capacity.note: Not addressed.

Speed.note: Lead time is not modelled; aircraft-on-ground cost (about EUR 100,000/day) is discussed only as motivation, and build time appears only as a cost driver (SFF 2013).

tools.name: Baumers et al. (2017) total-cost and capacity-utilisation model (IJPR)
tools.developer: M. Baumers, P. Dickens, C. Tuck, R. Hague (University of Nottingham), with L. Beltrametti and A. Gasparre on the 2017 paper
tools.context: Technology adoption: DMLS vs. machining+welding for a packaging-machine blower (2017); DMLS vs. EBM productivity and economies of scale (2016)
tools.processes: L-PBF (DMLS), EB-PBF (EBM)
tools.availability: Published models (Technol. Forecast. Soc. Change 102 (2016) 193-201; Int J Prod Res 55(23) (2017) 6957-6970; arXiv 1706.02090); in-house C++ packing/build-time tool not public
tools.description: Activity-based production cost models that combine direct costs with time-allocated indirect (machine and overhead) costs, voxel-based build-time estimates, and computational packing of the build volume. The 2017 version adds per-layer build-failure risk and the discounted value of design adaptation. It shows single-geometry builds overstate unit cost by 157% on average compared with full mixed builds.

NRE.note: Design and redesign re-validation costs are explicitly excluded; only per-build machine setup labour (180 min) is included (IJPR 2017 full text).

Production.note: Unit cost = material + energy + time-based indirect cost + setup and post-processing labour; the 17-4PH blower costs ~EUR 56-58/unit in mixed builds (IJPR 2017).

QA_Qual.note: Qualification and re-validation costs are not quantified (IJPR 2017).

QA_Insp.note: Inspection is only lumped into 37 min/part of manual post-processing labour, along with support removal, surface finishing and washing (IJPR 2017).

Storage.note: In-process inventory excluded (IJPR 2017).

Shared_Capital.note: Central contribution: indirect machine cost is allocated by build time and volume share, and filling unused build volume with other geometries ('fungible' capacity) cuts unit cost. Machine productivity is the principal cost driver (TFSC 2016; IJPR 2017).

Shared_Capacity.note: Filling builds with other users' parts is treated only as a cost effect; no lead-time or multi-site capacity analysis.

Speed.note: Lead time explicitly excluded (IJPR 2017).

Build time is computed from build-envelope and part dimensions using 2D/3D packing.

tools.name: Laureijs/Fuchs (CMU) process-based cost model: metal AM vs. forging
tools.developer: R. E. Laureijs, J. Bonnín Roca, S. P. Narra, C. Montgomery, J. L. Beuth, E. R. H. Fuchs (Carnegie Mellon University; E. R. H. Fuchs lab, Engineering & Public Policy)
tools.context: GE jet-engine bracket (design from public GE competition), commercial aviation, 1,000-12,000 brackets/yr; AM part redesigned ~80% lighter (1.66 kg saved). A footnote notes that military field repair, where forged spares cannot be sent for, would change the comparison.
tools.processes: Ti-6Al-4V by L-PBF (DMLS, EOS M290) and EBM (Arcam S12; Q20 discussed) vs. forging + heat treatment + grinding + multi-axis milling + wire EDM
tools.availability: Journal article: ASME J. Manuf. Sci. Eng. 139(8):081010, 2017, doi:10.1115/1.4035420. The full text was readable on the ASME Digital Collection page; supplementary input tables were not.
tools.description: Process-based cost model built on data from 14 anonymous firms (AM producers, powder and equipment suppliers, a university lab) and the Forging Industry Association. The AM route is modelled from the build step through stress relief (DMLS only), wire EDM, HIP, shot peening and destructive testing. At 1,000/yr the AM bracket costs about $3,200 vs. about $400 forged. With a 10-year fuel-saving NPV ($1,300 base, up to $3,000 per bracket), AM is competitive at 2,000-12,000/yr. Powder price and batch size (set by build orientation) are the top sensitivities. Cutting destructive testing from 1 part in 8 to 1 in 100 saves about $150/bracket at 10,000/yr, and about $410 when combined with vertical builds. FAA configuration control is modelled as 'one machine, one part' dedication of the AM machines.

NRE.note: Explicitly excluded. The model assumes the user has already optimised the design and converted it to STL, and it begins at the build step. Redesign enters only as the lighter geometry; its engineering cost is not counted (ASME full text).

Production.note: Per-bracket cost for DMLS, EBM and forging vs. annual volume (1,000-12,000/yr), with process-step inputs, reject rates, and best/base/worst ranges (ASME full text, Figs. 4-7).

QA_Qual.note: FAA production certification and configuration control are not costed in dollars. They are represented as a 'one machine, one part' dedication rule that raises AM machine cost per part below ~2,000/yr. Recertification after process changes is discussed only qualitatively (ASME full text).

QA_Insp.note: Destructive testing is explicitly modelled as a yield loss (base 1 part in 8 destroyed), with a sensitivity sweep (Fig. 8: 1:8 to 1:100 saves ~$150/bracket at 10k/yr). Testing time and equipment are not costed, and NDI/CT is not costed for AM (forging is assumed to use NDT). Borderline Yes for destructive testing only (ASME full text).

Storage.note: Inventory and spares are not analysed. Lead-time reduction appears only in the introduction, plus a footnote on military field repair (ASME full text).

Shared_Capital.note: Machine dedication is an explicit decision rule: AM machines are dedicated to the bracket, while forging equipment is shared with other parts. Batch size per build, which depends on vertical vs. horizontal orientation, is analysed for its cost effect (Fig. 9; ~$260 extra saving). The amortisation period is not stated in the text (ASME full text).

Shared_Capacity.note: Single-site production; no pooling of capacity across sites or users (ASME full text).

Speed.note: Time value is not modelled. The lifecycle benefit is fuel savings from weight reduction, not availability (ASME full text).

sources.title: Laureijs et al. (2017) Metal Additive Manufacturing: Cost Competitive Beyond Low Volumes, J. Manuf. Sci. Eng. 139(8):081010 - ASME Digital Collection full text
Same article - abstract (ScienceGate)
Sequeira (2017) IST thesis extended abstract citing Laureijs et al. for certification context

tools.name: Bonnín Roca (CMU) process-based cost model + facility-location model for decentralized metal AM
tools.developer: J. Bonnín Roca, P. Vaishnav, R. E. Laureijs, J. Mendonça, E. R. H. Fuchs (Carnegie Mellon University EPP; Universidade de Lisboa / IN+ via CMU Portugal; Bonnín Roca now at TU Eindhoven). M. G. Morgan is not a co-author of this paper; he co-authored the team's regulation papers.
tools.context: Commercial-aviation maintenance spare parts. Case is a non-flight-critical titanium jet-engine bracket (the GE-competition bracket from Laureijs et al. 2017) supplied to airports, under current-technology, performance-improvement and equipment-cost-drop scenarios.
tools.processes: Metal AM of Ti-6Al-4V (powder-bed; specific machine not visible in accessed text) with post-processing including HIP
tools.availability: Journal article: Additive Manufacturing 28 (2019) 136-151, doi:10.1016/j.addma.2019.04.010 (paywalled; abstract, keywords and section snippets accessed). Related CMU dissertation: Bonnín Roca (2017) 'Leaders and Followers: Challenges and Opportunities in the Adoption of Metal Additive Manufacturing Technologies' (CMU repository record; PDF host blocked this session).
tools.description: A location-dependent process-based cost model (local labour and land costs) feeds an uncapacitated facility-location MILP. The MILP picks the cost-minimising number and location of AM sites, trading production scale economies against transport and inventory costs. The optimal number of sites barely changes across technology-improvement scenarios, and as demand grows the factory moves toward the highest-demand airports. Decentralisation pays only for non-critical parts that can share the same equipment with minimal certification requirements, at combined volumes in the tens of thousands per year. At lower volumes it pays only for parts that need no HIP. Expensive post-processing equipment is what favours centralisation.

NRE.note: Only the abstract, section snippets and news pieces were read; they do not say whether design or build-preparation cost is included, although the predecessor Laureijs model excludes it.

Production.note: Location-dependent PBCM of metal AM production, including post-processing such as HIP (ScienceDirect abstract and snippets; CMU news).

QA_Qual.note: Certification is a scoping and scenario assumption rather than a cost. The model is limited to non-critical parts with 'minimal certification requirements' that can run on shared equipment (the CMU news piece states many part types are assumed to share one machine). This is the reverse of Laureijs 2017's 'one machine, one part' rule. No qualification cost line is visible in the accessed text.

QA_Insp.note: The accessed abstract and snippets do not mention inspection or testing, and whether the Laureijs destructive-testing yield carries over could not be checked.

Storage.note: Inventory cost is an explicit term in the location trade-off, alongside production and transport (abstract). Safety-stock formulation not visible.

Shared_Capital.note: Scale economies per site are the core trade-off. Many part types are assumed to share the same AM equipment (CMU news), and costly post-processing (HIP) equipment favours fewer, shared sites (abstract; CMU news).

Shared_Capacity.note: The MILP chooses the number and location of sites as an uncapacitated facility-location problem. Pooling therefore shows up only through scale economies, transport and inventory cost; there is no capacity constraint and no lead-time or queue effect. Other uncapacitated location models in the survey are rated Partial.

Speed.note: Lead time enters only implicitly, through the transport and inventory costs of distance. There is no dollar value of downtime, readiness or lead time; the introduction cites lead-time reduction only as a motivation (ScienceDirect snippets).

tools.name: Knofius-van der Heijden-Zijm AHP spare-part screening (SINTAS; Fokker, Royal Netherlands forces)
tools.developer: N. Knofius, M. C. van der Heijden, W. H. M. Zijm (University of Twente)
tools.context: After-sales service logistics; aviation spare-parts case (airplane-type attribute); large assortments, over 1,000 positive business cases found
tools.processes: Generic AM (material type and part size as go/no-go gates)
tools.availability: Published method (J. Manuf. Technol. Manag. 27(7):915-931; also Ch. 2 of Knofius 2019 PhD thesis, open PDF)
tools.description: Two-level AHP. Company goals (secure supply, reduce downtime, reduce costs) weight part attributes that can be pulled from company databases: safety-stock cost, manufacturing/order cost, demand rate, survival probability, remaining usage period, resupply lead time and airplane type. Go/no-go gates on material and size come first, and the ranking tells the firm which parts to build AM business cases for.

NRE.note: No criterion for 3D data, reverse engineering or redesign effort (thesis Tables 2.1/2.5).

Production.note: Conventional manufacturing/order cost is a scored attribute (17%), used as a proxy for savings potential; no AM cost estimate.

QA_Qual.note: Qualification and certification are not scored; the thesis notes certification cost was high in one case but left it out of the model.

QA_Insp.note: Not addressed.

Storage.note: Safety-stock cost is the highest-weighted attribute (18%) in the screening score. It is a criterion, not an inventory model.

Shared_Capital.note: Not addressed.

Shared_Capacity.note: Not addressed.

Speed.note: Resupply lead time (13%) and a 'reduce downtime' goal are in the AHP hierarchy; downtime is not dollarized.

tools.name: Paderborn DMRC Trade-off Methodology (TOM), 2017 version (Kruse, Reiher & Koch)
tools.developer: C. Lindemann, T. Reiher, U. Jahnke, R. Koch; A. Kruse (Paderborn University, DMRC)
tools.context: Workshop-based screening of existing parts, mainly aerospace (ESA projects; 90% overlap with independent expert selections)
tools.processes: Metal and polymer PBF (aerospace metal focus)

tools.description: Three-phase workshop (information, assessment, decision) in which non-experts and AM experts score candidate parts in a trade-off matrix. Criteria cover size limits, part class, assembly suppression, post-processing need, material applicability, design rules, property improvement and processing time, then material change, buy-to-fly, lead time and an AM-vs-milling cost ratio. Redesign and economic evaluation follow, and the 2017 revision adds knock-out gates and four value categories.

NRE.note: Redesign requirement-gathering is part of the method and redesign savings are discussed, but redesign and data-preparation effort are not costed (SFF 2014; RPJ 2015).

Production.note: A relative AM-vs-milling cost ratio and an early cost-estimation module feed the decision phase; a full cost comparison is only planned in the 2017 version (SFF 2014; SFF 2017).

QA_Qual.note: Material applicability (industry use, public data) and space-specific requirements are scored; no formal certification step (SFF 2014; SFF 2017).

QA_Insp.note: Not a criterion.

Storage.note: Savings on tooling and tool warehousing are mentioned, and the 2017 questionnaire asks about spare-part management strategy; no spares-inventory criterion.

Shared_Capital.note: Machine availability (in-house or provider) is only a size-feasibility check.

Shared_Capacity.note: Not addressed.

Speed.note: Lead, process and post-processing time, and time-criticality, are scored criteria (SFF 2014).

tools.name: VTT/Aalto digital spare parts program (DIVA / DIVALIITO): screening, metal PBF cost tool, qualification workflow
tools.developer: M. Salmi, J. Partanen, J. Tuomi, S. Chekurov, N. Kretzschmar et al. (Aalto University); S. Metsä-Kortelainen, A. Jussila et al. (VTT)

tools.description: Four-phase spare-part classification adapted from Knofius et al.: technical (material, size), photo-based geometry review, ranking, then economic (price, resupply lead time, annual consumption, MOQ). Only ~2% of one firm's items were feasible. It adds an STL-based metal PBF cost tool and illustrative AM vs. conventional business cases that include downtime. Its cost tool was later released as AMDSP 2.0, which is listed separately.

NRE.note: 3D-model availability is listed as a technical criterion; digitisation and redesign are not costed.

Production.note: MATLAB STL-based metal PBF cost tool: machine amortisation (8 yr), labour, material, packing ratio, powder recycling, follow-up time. Case costs include an Inconel 718 pin at ~EUR 55 vs. EUR 90.

QA_Qual.note: Certified printers and processes, approvals, and liability for safety-critical parts are discussed as barriers; not costed.

QA_Insp.note: The DIVA report lists hardness, porosity, Charpy, tensile, chemistry and functional tests on printed parts, but does not cost them.

Storage.note: The enclosure business case quantifies inventory reduction from printing on demand: average stock 10 vs 1 pcs, storage cost EUR 100 vs EUR 1, plus replenishment batch and logistics-to-stock costs (DIVA report Table 4). This is the same case that supports the Speed rating.

Shared_Capital.note: The PBF cost tool depreciates the printer over 8 years, but the 74% figure is the powder packing ratio, not part nesting. No utilisation, operating-hours or parts-per-build input is described. Spreading capital through service providers' 'wider customer base' is mentioned only qualitatively (DIVA report).

Shared_Capacity.note: The companion survey (Kretzschmar et al. 2018) sketches centralized and distributed digital spare-part network scenarios qualitatively.

Speed.note: The enclosure business case quantifies downtime (EUR 1,000/h) and a 20-day delivery time to show AM can be cheaper overall; re-supply lead time is a screening criterion.

QA_Qual.note: Prescribes qualification activities by class: full vs reduced QMP; statistically based material property suite for A/B vs simplified for C; preproduction articles required for A/B and removed for C; NASA attendance at the AM Readiness Review only for A1/A2. These are countable activities, but the standard gives no costs (Sec. 4.3, 4.15, 5, 6).

QA_Insp.note: Requires quantitative full surface and volumetric NDE for Class A (AMR-17) and removes NDE for Class C. Witness testing is set per Tables 5–8 for A/B, and Class C needs two tensile coupons per production build. Continuous production gets reduced witness sampling (Sec. 4.8, 4.11). The witness tables were not fully read.

Storage.note: Not addressed.

Shared_Capital.note: Explicitly spreads one-time qualification across parts: a QMP is registered to a machine, and a lot-mature material property suite applies to any part of any class built under an equivalently controlled QMP. Sub-QMPs allow reduced testing. NASA briefings hope NRE per new program will be 'dramatically reduced' by a shared AM ecosystem. All of this is qualitative (Sec. 3.2; Glendening et al. 2021).

Shared_Capacity.note: Not addressed.

Speed.note: Schedule mentioned only qualitatively ('building this foundation can take years'; witness tests 'can take considerable time') in the 2021 NASA QLF briefing.

tools.description: Sets durability and damage-tolerance certification requirements for metal AM structural parts by ASIP category (Fracture Critical Traceable/Non-Traceable, Durability Critical, Normal Controls), using equivalent initial damage size at category-specific exceedance probabilities and validated NDI capability. It recommends gaining experience in order of escalating criticality (NC, then DC, then FC).

NRE.note: Requires demonstrated process control (equipment qualification, software version control, periodic requalification, frozen process), which implies parameter development, but this is not costed (EZ-SB-19-01 process control section).

Production.note: Not addressed; cost appears only as stability/supportability criteria ('predictable costs', 'cost-effective' inspection).

QA_Qual.note: Sets class-specific analysis criteria: EIDS exceedance of 1e-1 (NC) and 1e-3 (DC), plus damage-tolerance analysis with a 1e-7 rogue EIDS for FC. All test frequencies, EIDS test counts and dissection plans are 'as approved by the procuring agency', so the qualification campaign by class cannot be costed from the bulletin.

QA_Insp.note: For all AM parts, requires NDI with POD at 95% confidence, dissection or validated in-process monitoring, coupons from production parts, and dimensional checks. These are not differentiated by part category, and frequencies are left to the procuring agency, so per-part inspection cannot be costed from the document.

Storage.note: Not addressed.

Shared_Capital.note: Recommends building certification experience from NC to DC to FC parts, each stage reusing earlier data, so qualification data is implicitly reused across parts. Not costed.

Shared_Capacity.note: Not addressed.

Speed.note: Only says sustainment NDI should be available 'in a timely manner'.

tools.processes: Metal L-PBF and DED; polymers (separate approved-materials lists)
tools.availability: Guidance letter publicly posted (NCMS AMMO); Tech Pubs not publicly accessed; public briefings (NRC, NSRP)
tools.description: Part failure-consequence severity (NAVSEA 5100.12-M Levels 1–7/N/A) determines whether material selection requirements and process/material qualification apply, whether a Technical Data Package is needed, and who approves. The process Tech Pubs then prescribe procedure qualification, part verification builds and a production conformance test plan.

NRE.note: A DED Procedure defining essential variables must be NAVSEA-approved before testing, and a TDP is required for Levels 1–6. Not costed (Hovanec 2021; Ser 05T/2018-024).

Production.note: Not in the framework. NAVSEA says NAVSUP's separate cost/part tool is being integrated into TDP development (Rettaliata 2020); see Spillover.

QA_Insp.note: NDE is set by material group with MIL-STD-2035 Class 1 acceptance; production NDE and destructive-test schedules are defined per part in each Production Conformance Evaluation Plan, not by severity level. In-situ monitoring in place of NDE is a stated goal (Rettaliata 2017).

Storage.note: Not addressed in the framework.

Shared_Capital.note: Explicit: procedure qualification is done once per process/material combination and applies to any geometry if essential elements are kept, so it spreads across parts. Not costed (Hovanec 2021).

Shared_Capacity.note: Not addressed.

Speed.note: The guidance letter says only qualitatively that AM 'can shorten the design-to-production cycle'.

tools.description: Metal AM build-prep software (part positioning, supports, lattices, print strategies). Shared_Capacity.note: As build-preparation software for a single machine's builds, 3DXpert does not address capacity pooled across sites or users.

tools.name: Ansys Additive Prep (Cost Estimator)
tools.developer: Ansys, now part of Synopsys (ansys.com product pages redirect to ansys.synopsys.com); Additive Prep runs inside Ansys SpaceClaim
tools.context: General metal LPBF build preparation; no defense user found
tools.processes: Metal laser powder bed fusion. Cost data is built into SLM machine profiles only; other machine profiles show zero machine cost.
tools.availability: Commercial license (SpaceClaim-based Ansys additive tools)
tools.description: Build-preparation tool whose Cost Estimator prices the whole build job. Machine cost comes from build time (laser path and jump times plus recoater time per layer). Material is powder volume over the baseplate area times part height, times density, plus a material-loss %. A profit margin is added. Output is an 'Estimated Total Price' exportable to CSV.

NRE.note: Supports and scan-pattern build files are generated here, but preparation effort is not costed (Ansys help 2024 R2).

Production.note: Build-job cost from scan-path build time, machine cost, powder use with loss % and profit; build-level total, no per-part split (Ansys help 2024 R2).

QA_Qual.note: The cost-estimator help lists only machine, material and profit terms, and Additive Prep's documented build-preparation scope does not include qualification.

QA_Insp.note: The cost-estimator help lists only machine, material and profit terms, with no inspection step.

Storage.note: Additive Prep prepares and prices single build jobs, so inventory is outside its documented scope.

Shared_Capital.note: Machine cost (largest contributor) is spread over everything in the build volume, so packing more parts lowers unit cost implicitly; no amortization or utilization inputs documented (Ansys help 2024 R2).

Shared_Capacity.note: Additive Prep prices one build job on one machine and does not address capacity shared across sites or users.

Speed.note: The help computes build time only to cost the machine and does not output lead time or a value of earlier delivery.

tools.name: Ulu-Huang-Kara-Whitefoot (CMU) concurrent structure + process-parameter optimization for minimum-cost metal AM
tools.developer: E. Ulu, R. Huang, L. B. Kara, K. S. Whitefoot (Carnegie Mellon University, Mechanical Engineering)
tools.context: Design-stage optimisation of structural parts (cantilever, L-beam, bracket, table) for EBM. Cost inputs come from 14 US EBM Ti64 producers at >=13,500 units/yr.
tools.processes: EBM (electron-beam powder bed fusion), Ti-6Al-4V
tools.availability: Journal paper (ASME J. Mechanical Design per author page); author-hosted PDF
tools.description: Couples a process-based cost model (material with 1% scrap, machine investment and maintenance amortised over 7 yr at 7,000 h/yr, energy, labour, 3.5% reject factor) with SIMP topology optimisation. Beam power is chosen per element, so structure and process parameters are optimised together for minimum cost under compliance constraints. Concurrent optimisation cuts cost by up to ~15% and build time by ~21% vs. structure-only optimisation.

NRE.note: Design, build-preparation and parameter-development effort are not costed. The tool automates part of DfAM, but its cost is not counted (author PDF).

Production.note: Per-part cost from build time (scan passes, power, velocity), material, energy and labour; e.g. bracket $675 to $575 (author PDF, Table 3).

QA_Qual.note: Not addressed (author PDF).

QA_Insp.note: A single 3.5% reject-rate factor is said to cover quality control and destructive testing. There are no separate inspection or testing line items (author PDF).

Storage.note: Not addressed.

Shared_Capital.note: Machine investment is amortised over 7 years at 7,000 h/yr. Packing, batch size and orientation are explicitly excluded (author PDF).

Shared_Capacity.note: Not addressed.

Speed.note: Build time is reported as an outcome but is not valued or linked to part availability (author PDF).

sources.title: Ulu, Huang, Kara, Whitefoot - Concurrent Structure and Process Optimization for Minimum Cost Metal Additive Manufacturing (author-hosted PDF)

tools.name: Nie-Jung-Kara-Whitefoot (CMU) part-consolidation optimization for minimum production cost/time with metal AM
tools.developer: Z. Nie, S. Jung, L. B. Kara, K. S. Whitefoot (Carnegie Mellon University)
tools.context: Aircraft aft-fairing assembly (48 components, 94 riveted interfaces) supplied by an aircraft-industry partner; decides which components to merge into AM parts
tools.processes: Ti-6Al-4V by EBM powder bed fusion and by wire-fed electron-beam DED; Al-6061 in comparison scenarios
tools.availability: ASME journal paper (J. Mechanical Design per file name); PDF hosted by CMU Whitefoot group; related US patent 'Tool for optimal part consolidation selection for AM' (not opened)
tools.description: Generates consolidation candidates from an interface connectivity matrix and removes structurally redundant ones with a 'closed-loop filter'. It then optimises build orientation for minimum support, places parts with a 2-D bottom-left layout, and estimates cost or time; a genetic algorithm searches large assemblies. Consolidating 17 components into 4 parts minimises cost (~20% lower unit cost); merging into 2 parts minimises time (~25%). Full consolidation is rarely optimal because support material and removal costs rise.

NRE.note: Redesign and engineering effort for consolidated parts is not costed (CMU PDF).

Production.note: Unit cost from part and support material, machine and maintenance, scrap, energy, setup, support removal, plus assembly (machining, riveting) for unconsolidated interfaces (CMU PDF).

QA_Qual.note: Not addressed (CMU PDF).

QA_Insp.note: Inspection is not modelled (CMU PDF).

Storage.note: Inventory is explicitly excluded. Fewer part numbers could cut spares inventory, but this is not modelled (CMU PDF).

Shared_Capital.note: Machine cost is an hourly rate (amortised equipment, maintenance, labour) times build time, and setup cost depends on the number of batches from the plate layout; utilisation and sharing with other part numbers are not modelled (CMU PDF).

Shared_Capacity.note: Not addressed.

Speed.note: Unit production time is an alternative objective (time-optimal consolidation). Time is not dollarised or tied to when parts are needed (CMU PDF).

sources.title: Nie, Jung, Kara, Whitefoot - Optimization of Part Consolidation for Minimum Production Costs and Time Using Additive Manufacturing (CMU-hosted PDF)

tools.name: Piili et al. (LUT/Aalto) laser PBF stainless-steel cost estimation by build scenario
tools.developer: H. Piili, A. Happonen, T. Väistö, V. Venkataramanan, J. Partanen, A. Salminen (affiliations not shown on the accessed record; record held by Aalto University)
tools.context: Generic stainless-steel parts on a research L-PBF machine equivalent to EOS M-series; extreme build scenarios (single part vs. full build)
tools.processes: L-PBF ('laser additive manufacturing'), stainless steel
tools.availability: Conference paper, Physics Procedia 78 (2015) 388-396, doi:10.1016/j.phpro.2015.11.053 (open access; only abstract and a review summary accessed)
tools.description: Estimates part cost from build time, machine, material and energy across build scenarios with optimised machine utilisation. Machine investment dominates while energy and material are minor, so time per part is the main lever. A secondary review reports that building as many parts as possible per build cut cost 81-92% vs. building singly.

NRE.note: Only the abstract and a review summary were read; neither says whether design or build-preparation effort is costed.

Production.note: Per-part cost from build time, machine, material and energy (Aaltodoc abstract).

QA_Qual.note: Only the abstract and a review summary were read; neither says whether qualification is costed.

QA_Insp.note: Only the abstract and a review summary were read; neither says whether inspection or post-processing is costed.

Storage.note: Outside the documented scope: the paper estimates per-part cost by build scenario from build time, machine, material and energy (Aaltodoc abstract).

Shared_Capital.note: Machine utilisation is optimised and build scenarios are compared (Aaltodoc abstract). A 2024 MDPI review reports that 40 concurrent items cut the machine-cost share by 6%, and that full builds cut cost 81-92% vs. single-part builds.

Shared_Capacity.note: Outside the documented scope: one research machine's build scenarios are costed, with no multi-site or multi-user capacity (Aaltodoc abstract).

Speed.note: Outside the documented scope: time per part is treated only as a cost driver, not as a lead-time value (Aaltodoc abstract).

sources.title: Piili et al. (2015) Cost Estimation of Laser Additive Manufacturing of Stainless Steel - Aaltodoc record/abstract
Cost Modelling for Powder Bed Fusion and Directed Energy Deposition AM (MDPI J. Manuf. Mater. Process. 8(4):142, 2024) - review summarising Piili

tools.name: Barclift et al. (Penn State) CAD-integrated cost estimation and build-orientation optimization for metal PBF
tools.developer: M. Barclift, A. Armstrong, T. W. Simpson, S. B. Joshi (Pennsylvania State University)
tools.context: Design-stage cost estimate inside SolidWorks for a metal-printed automotive component. Distinct from the 2016 powder-reuse entry, whose depreciation model it reuses: this paper adds CAD-API support generation and build-orientation and packing effects.
tools.processes: Metal powder bed fusion
tools.availability: ASME IDETC/CIE 2017 paper DETC2017-68376 (43rd Design Automation Conf.); SolidWorks API macro (not public). Abstract only accessed.
tools.description: Pulls part volume and surfaces through the SolidWorks API and generates internal and external supports as solid bodies, then varies build orientation. This lets designers estimate build time and feedstock (including depreciation of reused powder) while designing. An imprecise support angle underestimates support volume by 34% and build time by 20%. Poor orientation and packing can push powder-depreciation cost to nearly twice the material cost.

NRE.note: Only the abstract was read; it automates support generation and orientation but does not say whether design or build-preparation labour is costed, and the 2016 base model does cost per-part geometry preparation.

Production.note: Build time and feedstock, including supports and powder depreciation, per part (Penn State abstract).

QA_Qual.note: The abstract scopes the estimator to build time and feedstock (supports, powder depreciation) inside CAD, which excludes qualification.

QA_Insp.note: The abstract scopes the estimator to build time and feedstock, so inspection lies outside its documented scope.

Storage.note: Not addressed.

Shared_Capital.note: Packing within the build volume is shown to drive powder-depreciation cost. Machine-time sharing and amortisation are not described in the abstract (Penn State abstract; MDPI review).

Shared_Capacity.note: Not addressed.

Speed.note: Build time is a cost driver only.

sources.title: Barclift, Armstrong, Simpson, Joshi (2017) CAD-Integrated cost estimation and build orientation optimization to support design for metal AM - Penn State record/abstract
MDPI JMMP 2024 cost-modelling review summarising Barclift et al. 2016 and 2017

tools.name: Budinoff & Shafae geometry-to-cost process-based model for metal L-PBF design alternatives
tools.developer: H. D. Budinoff, M. Shafae (affiliation not shown on accessed page)
tools.context: Choosing among geometrically different design alternatives of the same function for L-PBF
tools.processes: Metal L-PBF plus post-processing
tools.availability: Journal article, Int. J. Adv. Manuf. Technol. 121:6125-6136 (2022); abstract accessed
tools.description: Process-based cost model of the L-PBF build and post-processing, applied to design alternatives. Costs differ by up to 14% between alternatives, with part mass and build time the strongest predictors. Higher complexity was linked to lower cost but not strongly to reject rates. Scrap and reject rates vary with geometry in conflicting directions.

NRE.note: Only the Springer abstract was read; it does not say whether design or build-preparation cost is part of the process-based model.

Production.note: Per-part cost of build and post-processing by geometry (Springer abstract).

QA_Qual.note: Only the abstract was read; qualification is not mentioned, so whether it is costed cannot be established.

QA_Insp.note: The abstract shows scrap and reject rates vary with geometry but does not say whether inspection or testing is costed.

Storage.note: Not addressed.

Shared_Capital.note: Only the abstract was read; it does not show how machine cost is amortised or whether parts share a build.

Shared_Capacity.note: Not addressed.

Speed.note: The abstract scopes the model to build and post-processing cost of design alternatives; time enters only as build time, a cost predictor.

sources.title: Budinoff & Shafae (2022) Connecting part geometry and cost for metal powder bed fusion, IJAMT 121

tools.name: Sartini et al. (UNIVPM) analytic cost model for bound metal deposition
tools.developer: M. Sartini, I. Bianchi, A. Vita, M. Germani, M. Mandolini (Università Politecnica delle Marche)
tools.context: Designer-facing cost estimate for metal material extrusion. Validated on a 17-4 PH tensile specimen on a Desktop Metal Studio System (estimate within 2% of actual).
tools.processes: Bound metal deposition (metal material extrusion + debind + sinter)
tools.availability: Open-access conference paper, DESIGN 2024 (Proc. Design Society), doi:10.1017/pds.2024.184
tools.description: Analytic per-part cost over pre-processing, printing, debinding and sintering. Each phase sums material, machine, labour, energy and consumables, driven by part and support geometry, material, batch quantity and accuracy. Sintering machine and energy dominate the validation case (EUR 565 estimated vs. EUR 576 actual).

NRE.note: Pre-processing labour (setup, nesting and job preparation) is costed. Design and parameter development are not (Cambridge PDF).

Production.note: Full per-part phase-by-phase cost (Cambridge PDF).

QA_Qual.note: Not modelled (Cambridge PDF).

QA_Insp.note: Not modelled (Cambridge PDF).

Storage.note: Not addressed.

Shared_Capital.note: Machine hourly rate covers depreciation, overhead and maintenance at a 57% load factor. Job preparation and debind/sinter costs are divided across parts in the batch (Cambridge PDF).

Shared_Capacity.note: Not addressed.

Speed.note: Not addressed.

sources.title: Sartini et al. (2024) An analytic cost model for bound metal deposition, DESIGN 2024

tools.name: DeBoer-Diba-Hosseini AM cost calculator (FFF and metal bound powder extrusion)
tools.developer: B. DeBoer, F. Diba, A. Hosseini (Ontario Tech University; Fleming College CAMIIT)
tools.context: Feasibility of AM vs. traditional manufacture. Metal case is a topology-optimised double-cardan H-yoke in 17-4 PH on a Markforged Metal X.
tools.processes: Bound powder extrusion (metal) and FFF (polymer)
tools.availability: Open-access CSME 2021 congress paper
tools.description: Cost calculator covering machine (equipment cost over a payback period and operating hours, power, changeover and setup labour), material (adjusted for shrinkage), post-processing (wash, sinter, argon, debind fluid, loading labour), overhead and profit. In the H-yoke case about 85% of part cost was Metal X capital, so BPE was judged uneconomic unless weight is critical.

NRE.note: Not addressed (UPEI PDF).

Production.note: Per-part cost for the metal BPE route (UPEI PDF).

QA_Qual.note: Not addressed.

QA_Insp.note: Not addressed.

Storage.note: Not addressed.

Shared_Capital.note: Equipment cost is spread over payback period and assumed operating hours. Packing in wash and sinter is noted only qualitatively (UPEI PDF).

Shared_Capacity.note: Not addressed.

Speed.note: Not addressed.

sources.title: DeBoer, Diba, Hosseini (2021) Design and Development of a Cost Calculator for Additive Manufacturing, CSME 2021

tools.name: Reiher et al. (Paderborn DMRC) holistic approach: part selection through test and verification
tools.developer: T. Reiher, C. Lindemann, U. Jahnke, G. Deppe, R. Koch (Paderborn University, DMRC)
tools.context: Industrialising AM from candidate selection to verified part; space case (satellite reaction-wheel bracket). Extends the TOM matrix scored in the main file.
tools.processes: Metal powder-bed AM (alloy not named)
tools.availability: Journal article, Progress in Additive Manufacturing 2:43-55 (2017), open-access PDF
tools.description: Chains the TOM selection matrix (rough cost quote, knock-out criteria, scored sub-criteria) with topology-optimisation redesign, a manufacturing strategy (orientation, supports, thermal stress) and part marking. It adds a three-tier test scheme: part-independent material/process tests, witness specimens in every build, and part-specific NDT (CT, dimensional, surface) plus load tests. The bracket was 60% lighter with buy-to-fly reduced from ~50 to 1.5. AM was cheaper at the forecast volume, although post-processing and quality costs 'had a major impact'.

NRE.note: Redesign workflow (FE topology optimisation, voxel smoothing, NURBS) is defined, but its effort is not costed (Springer PDF).

Production.note: TOM gives a rough cost quote, and a DMRC costing tool compared production, self- and lifecycle costs. The paper reports the conclusion but no cost figures (Springer PDF).

QA_Qual.note: Explicit qualification steps: fundamental material/process testing, frozen SOPs, and part-specific readiness testing at qualification loads. Not costed (Springer PDF).

QA_Insp.note: Per-build witness specimens (tensile, density) and per-part CT/dimensional/surface NDT are prescribed. Quality costs are said to be major but are not itemised (Springer PDF).

Storage.note: Qualitative: only raw material needs stocking, which reduces inventory, WIP and capital lock-up. On-demand JIT production at the assembly point is proposed (Springer PDF).

Shared_Capital.note: Qualitative: high machine prices favour centralised production with machines near full workload. TOM's rough quote rests on depreciation-time assumptions (Springer PDF).

Shared_Capacity.note: Qualitative: distributed production would need more machines and more suitable parts; low build rates require buffer inventory (Springer PDF).

Speed.note: Qualitative lead-time reduction from on-demand production for a part designed late but installed early. Not quantified (Springer PDF).

sources.title: Reiher et al. (2017) Holistic approach for industrializing AM technology: from part selection to test and verification, Prog. Addit. Manuf. 2:43-55

tools.name: Siller et al. (TU Berlin) potential-assessment and adaptation method for AM of conventionally made components
tools.developer: N. Siller, S. Werner, V. Molina, D. Göhlich (Technische Universität Berlin, Institute of Machine Design and Systems Technology)
tools.context: Screening an existing portfolio for AM with stakeholder-weighted criteria. Demonstrated on an 11-part gas-turbine pilot-nozzle assembly for serviceability (direct spare replacement).
tools.processes: Powder bed fusion (metal L-PBF implied by cited standard and turbine case)
tools.availability: Open-access journal article, Research in Engineering Design 35:73-96
tools.description: A pass/fail prefilter (fits build space, material available, AM-sensitive features acceptable, no legal restriction, conventional production not much cheaper) is followed by 0-4 scored assessments. These cover in-process and post-process restrictions and 'opportunistic' economic, eco-social and functional drivers, weighted by utility analysis. An automatic 'AM adaptation potential' flags parts that minor redesign could make suitable. Below 40% overall means low suitability; above 65% means generally suitable. In the case, 5 of 11 parts failed the prefilter.

NRE.note: The adaptation-potential score flags where minor redesign would help, but redesign effort is not costed (Springer full text).

Production.note: Economics enter only as a prefilter check that conventional production is not much cheaper, and as 0-4 driver ratings. No cost is calculated (Springer full text).

QA_Qual.note: Not a criterion. Load-capacity simulation and testing follow the assessment (Springer full text).

QA_Insp.note: Post-processing need is scored, but inspection is not (Springer full text).

Storage.note: Table 7 scores 'Enables on-demand-manufacturing/build-to-order' and 'Secures/improves supply-chain activities' as 0-4 AM drivers, a qualitative proxy for stock avoidance; inventory is not named or costed (TU Berlin open-access PDF).

Shared_Capital.note: Not a criterion; build-space fit only (Springer full text).

Shared_Capacity.note: Company capacity is mentioned only for scheduling deferred parts (Springer full text).

Speed.note: Table 7 includes 'Reduces lead time' as a 0-4 scored AM driver; its weight was 0 in the turbine case for lack of production-time data, and lead time is never quantified (TU Berlin open-access PDF).

sources.title: Siller et al. (2023/2024) Method for potential assessment and adaptation for AM of conventionally manufactured components, Res. Eng. Des. 35

tools.name: Bracken et al. (Penn State) Geometry for Additive Part Selection (GAPS) worksheet
tools.developer: J. Bracken, T. Pomorski, C. Armstrong, R. Prabhu, T. W. Simpson, K. Jablokow, W. Cleary, N. A. Meisel (Pennsylvania State University)
tools.context: Helps engineers, drafters and designers with little AM knowledge flag good metal PBF candidates and avoid failed prints. Ratings compared with expert raters.
tools.processes: Metal powder bed fusion
tools.availability: Worksheet published in Additive Manufacturing 35:101163 (2020); presented in an nTopology webinar
tools.description: Paper worksheet that rates nine literature-backed geometric features known to affect metal PBF printability and totals them into a geometric-suitability score. Example components were rated and compared with expert assessments, and preliminary user feedback is reported.

NRE.note: The worksheet scores only nine geometric printability features (abstract; nTop blog), so design or engineering cost is outside its documented scope.

Production.note: The worksheet gives a geometric-suitability score only; failed prints and wasted material are cited as motivation, not costed (abstract; nTop blog).

QA_Qual.note: Not addressed.

QA_Insp.note: Not addressed.

Storage.note: Not addressed.

Shared_Capital.note: Not addressed.

Shared_Capacity.note: Not addressed.

Speed.note: Not addressed.

tools.name: Mitterbaur (TU Wien) data-driven spare-part identification for AM from digitized legacy drawings
tools.developer: M. Mitterbaur (advisor F. Ansari; co-advisor T. Madreiter), TU Wien Institute of Management Sciences
tools.context: Industrial spare-parts archives that hold only scanned legacy engineering drawings, a situation analogous to legacy defense TDPs
tools.processes: AM generally; material is extracted as an attribute, and metal focus is not stated
tools.availability: Diploma thesis (reposiTUm), proof-of-concept demonstrator; abstract accessed
tools.description: Uses deep-learning object detection and text recognition plus image processing to find title blocks and BOM tables in scanned drawings, convert them to a spreadsheet, and extract printability-relevant attributes. Assemblies and standard parts are then filtered out to shortlist AM spare-part candidates. Evaluated on an industrial use case.

NRE.note: The thesis digitises drawing title blocks and BOMs to screen parts; it does not estimate design, digitisation or reverse-engineering cost (open-access thesis, Ch. 1-3; the demonstrator chapter was not machine-readable).

Production.note: The stated objectives cover drawing digitisation and technical-attribute identification only; cost appears only in the literature review (thesis Ch. 1-3).

QA_Qual.note: Not addressed.

QA_Insp.note: Not addressed.

Storage.note: Inventory reduction motivates the thesis, but the objectives and demonstrator scope are drawing digitisation and filtering of standard parts and assemblies, with no inventory criterion (thesis Ch. 1-3).

Shared_Capital.note: Not addressed.

Shared_Capacity.note: Not addressed.

Speed.note: Not addressed.

sources.title: Mitterbaur (2023) A data-driven approach to identifying spare parts suitable for AM through the digitization of legacy engineering drawings (TU Wien)

tools.name: Lawand et al. (McGill/Chalmers/GKN) dynamic lifecycle-cost model for DED remanufacturing (repair/extend vs. replace)
tools.developer: L. Lawand, M. Panarotto, P. Andersson, O. Isaksson, M. Kokkolaras (McGill University; Chalmers University of Technology; GKN Aerospace Engine Systems)
tools.context: Aero-engine turbine rear structure. Choose between original, robust and 'adaptable' designs, where a stiffener is DED-deposited on-site mid-life to extend life instead of replacing the part.
tools.processes: Directed energy deposition (Inconel 718 stiffener)
tools.availability: Open-access journal article, Aerospace 7(8):110 (2020); model built in Simulink (not public)
tools.description: Present-value lifecycle cost over a 700-month service period, with nine categories: material, manufacturing (variable plus fixed tooling), transport (replacement only), fuel, replacement labour, failure-probability-based repair, inventory, salvage, and recertification (supplemental type certificate fee). Nested optimisation (MADS) picks the stiffener design and deposition time. Deposition timing dominates LCC, and the optimal design lifespan is 312-432 months.

NRE.note: Design and engineering cost of the adaptable design is not a separate term (MDPI full text).

Production.note: Material and manufacturing (per-cycle variable plus fixed tooling) and repair cost terms (MDPI full text).

QA_Qual.note: The only certification term is a fixed EASA supplemental-type-certificate issuance fee (gamma_recert, Eq. 11). No qualification testing, analysis or approval effort is modeled, so the term is a crude proxy for part of the burden (MDPI full text).

QA_Insp.note: Inspection and NDT are not separately modelled (MDPI full text).

Storage.note: Inventory is an explicit LCC category, but the accessed text does not show how inventory differs between on-site deposition and stocking replacements (MDPI full text).

Shared_Capital.note: DED machine capital is not modelled (MDPI full text).

Shared_Capacity.note: Not addressed.

Speed.note: Downtime and lead time are not modelled. Transport is costed only for replacement (MDPI full text).

sources.title: Lawand et al. (2020) Dynamic Lifecycle Cost Modeling for Adaptable Design Optimization of Additively Remanufactured Aeroengine Components, Aerospace 7(8):110
Peer-review report for the same paper (notes no public LCC model for DED repair existed)

tools.name: Xu & Feng AM-based remanufacturing cost model (remanufacture vs. new manufacture)
tools.developer: Y. Xu, W. Feng (Cranfield University, School of Applied Sciences)
tools.context: End-of-life decision: remanufacture a specified component by an AM-based process or make a new one
tools.processes: AM-based remanufacturing (deposition process and metal not named in abstract)
tools.availability: Open-access article, Journal of Remanufacturing 4:4 (2014), doi:10.1186/2210-4690-4-4 (abstract only accessed; publisher full text blocked)
tools.description: Framework and cost-breakdown structure for an AM-based remanufacturing process, validated by expert judgement, with a case comparing remanufacturing cost against new manufacture.

NRE.note: The open-access full text costs reverse engineering and data processing (labour-based) as pre-production elements of the cost breakdown.

Production.note: The cost breakdown covers setup, wire deposition (labour, shielding gas, material, depreciation, power), grinding and overhead for repairing Ti-6Al-4V slat-track lugs vs. making a new part (full text).

QA_Qual.note: No qualification or certification step or cost; expert judgement validates the cost model, not the part (full text).

QA_Insp.note: Inspection and testing are not in the cost breakdown; a 'Quality Grading' step in the process flow carries no cost (full text).

Storage.note: The model covers costs on the remanufacturing premises only and leaves inventory and reverse logistics to higher-level analysis (full text).

Shared_Capital.note: Deposition and grinding machine depreciation are charged by operating time with an idle-rate adjustment; there is no utilisation or shared-use analysis (full text).

Shared_Capacity.note: Capacity is not modelled (full text).

Speed.note: Lead time, delivery and downtime are not modelled; only machine idle rates appear (full text).

sources.title: Xu & Feng (2014) Develop a cost model to evaluate the economic benefit of remanufacturing based on specific technique - Aston research record
Same paper - Aston ePrints record

tools.name: Baffa (Univ. Florence) WAAM repair-vs-replace sustainability and remanufacturing-viability model
tools.developer: F. Baffa (Università degli Studi di Firenze, doctoral thesis)
tools.context: Hybrid WAAM repair of a mould insert, compared with replacement. Remanufacturing viability across three supply chains and three materials (steel, aluminium, titanium).
tools.processes: Hybrid WAAM (wire-arc DED + machining)
tools.availability: PhD thesis; full text embargoed until 31 Dec 2026 (abstract only)
tools.description: Develops WAAM repair toolpath strategies, compares the sustainability of repair vs. replacement, and builds a mathematical model of remanufacturing viability (cost and energy) in closed-loop supply chains. It identifies feasible configurations and the parameters that most affect cost and energy.

NRE.note: The thesis is embargoed until 31 Dec 2026 and the abstract does not say whether the effort of developing repair toolpath strategies is costed.

Production.note: Cost (and energy) of repair vs. replacement across materials (abstract).

QA_Qual.note: Only the abstract is public; it does not say whether requalification of repaired parts is costed.

QA_Insp.note: Only the abstract is public; it does not say whether inspection of the repaired insert is costed.

Storage.note: The abstract describes a remanufacturing model over three closed-loop supply chains but does not say whether inventory is costed.

Shared_Capital.note: Only the abstract is public; it does not say how WAAM or machining equipment cost is allocated.

Shared_Capacity.note: The abstract compares three supply-chain configurations but does not say whether repair capacity is shared or located across sites.

Speed.note: Only the abstract is public; it does not say whether repair vs. replacement lead time or downtime is valued.

sources.title: Baffa (2024) Repairing through Wire Arc Additive Manufacturing: dedicated strategies and sustainability assessment (FLORE record)

tools.name: Morgan & Prentiss (NPS) Navy AM item-identification approach and make-vs-buy comparison
tools.developer: J. A. Morgan, J. M. Prentiss (Naval Postgraduate School MBA Professional Report; advisors D. E. Brinkley, S. Tick)
tools.context: Navy afloat and shore supply chain (COSAL/WSS). Case: 40 phone-jack boxes for USS Whidbey Island printed at CDSA Dam Neck; >500 needed fleet-wide for outfitting.
tools.processes: Polymer FDM (ABS-ESD7, PC, ULTEM). Metal appears only as a machined-aluminium comparator, so this is outside the metal scope and was included at the brief's request.
tools.availability: NPS report (public, DTIC/Calhoun; archive.org copy read)
tools.description: Proposes three candidate lenses: frequency (demand-based, more than ~2 issues per 6 months), availability (hard to obtain), and criticality. O- and I-level parts are preferred; D-level is excluded. It applies a direct-material cost formula and relevant-cost make-vs-buy logic. AM in ABS-ESD7 cost $1,926.58 for 40 boxes with a 1-2 week lead time, vs. $1,802.70 for commercially machined aluminium (5 weeks) and $3,267.90 for ULTEM 2300 (5 weeks). It cites a 1-2 year approval process before printed parts go aboard.

NRE.note: Reverse engineering is flagged as an added cost risk but not quantified (archive.org PDF).

Production.note: Direct material cost formula only (model and support material by canister price); labour, machine and overhead are excluded (archive.org PDF).

QA_Qual.note: Qualitative: approval by multiple technical warrant holders, a 1-2 year qualification estimate (NSWC Carderock), and a list of nonmetallic tests (archive.org PDF).

QA_Insp.note: Per-part inspection is not costed (archive.org PDF).

Storage.note: Reduced holding and tool-set costs are argued, but holding costs are explicitly not quantified (archive.org PDF).

Shared_Capital.note: Fixed and machine costs are excluded (archive.org PDF).

Shared_Capacity.note: Qualitative: wholesale corresponds to centralised AM and retail to distributed AM. A lab supplier was excluded for lacking production capacity (archive.org PDF).

Speed.note: Lead times (AM 1-2 weeks vs. 5 weeks machined) sit beside costs in the make-vs-buy table, and the report asks whether the Navy will pay a premium for delivery. Not dollarised (archive.org PDF).

sources.title: Morgan & Prentiss (2014) An analysis of item identification for additive manufacturing (3-D printing) within the Naval supply chain (NPS) - full text
Same report - catalogue record

tools.name: DoDI 5000.93 Use of Additive Manufacturing in the DoD (Change 1, July 6, 2021)
tools.developer: OUSD(R&E) (approved by Barbara McQuiston); incorporates and cancels DTM-19-006
tools.context: DoD-wide policy for using AM in acquisition, maintenance and sustainment
tools.processes: Process-agnostic
tools.availability: Public (Executive Services Directorate issuance)
tools.description: The instruction requires a 'risk-informed approach' but prescribes no decision method, scoring model or cost-benefit tool. Maintenance activities must 'consider and evaluate AM's technical and economic practicality.' Contracts should identify parts that 'are, or could be, produced using AM.' Organizations that share approved AM data across organizations must adopt JAMMEX.

NRE.note: Directs buying only the AM data and license rights needed (§3.1.c) and flagging AM-capable parts in the bill of materials (§3.1.d). TDP creation and reverse engineering are not costed.

Production.note: Requires evaluating 'technical and economic practicality' (§3.3.c) but gives no cost method.

QA_Qual.note: Policies must define 'the level of qualification, certification, risk evaluation, and approval authority' for AM parts (§3.2.a). Not costed.

QA_Insp.note: Parts must 'comply with established quality control criteria' (§3.2.d), and AM data must include 'testing requirements and acceptance or rejection criteria' (§3.1.b(2)). Not costed.

Storage.note: Inventory or stock reduction is not addressed. JAMMEX is framed only as a data-sharing portal.

Shared_Capital.note: Not addressed.

Shared_Capacity.note: USD(A&S) must ensure 'adequate and uninterrupted AM capacity' in the domestic base (§2.3.e). Pooling across sites or units is not addressed.

Speed.note: Calls for making parts 'consistent with demand urgency' (§3.3.b) and in contingency or combat environments to improve readiness. Not quantified.

tools.name: RAND 3D printing supply-chain impact matrix and fab-lab concept (PE-229)
tools.developer: RAND Corporation (Simon Véronneau, Geoffrey Torrington, Jakub P. Hlavka)
tools.context: DoD and commercial supply chains. Military examples include forward operating bases, ships, submarines and contested theaters.
tools.processes: Technology-agnostic. The proposed fab-lab has CNC milling, metal-alloy AM, plastic-composite AM and CT metrology.
tools.availability: Public RAND Perspective PE-229 (22 pp.)
tools.description: A two-by-two matrix in which the impact of 3D printing grows with site isolation and with ad hoc (unpredictable) demand. The paper proposes a four-machine fab-lab and a process flow: incoming inspection, CT, 3D rendering, AM or CNC, post-production, outgoing inspection, tracking and serialization, then return to service. It calls for a total supply-chain cost comparison but gives no cost model and does not rank parts.

NRE.note: CT metrology can 'generate a 3D printable design' from existing parts. Characterizing a part without a 3D diagram 'would take about one hour.' Not costed.

Production.note: Says a fab-lab vs centralized comparison 'must involve a total supply chain cost approach' and calls for a 'comprehensive cost-effectiveness evaluation'. No per-part cost.

QA_Qual.note: Recommends 'rationalizing the certification and testing approach' for AM components. Qualitative.

QA_Insp.note: Incoming and outgoing inspection and CT scanning are steps in the process flow, and CT is called 'relatively underappreciated'. Not costed.

Storage.note: The full text does not discuss inventory, stock or holding cost; it mentions only secure storage of part design files.

Shared_Capital.note: The full text mentions civilian fab-labs used 'on a pay-per-use basis' but does not cost the proposed fab-lab or discuss sharing its equipment.

Shared_Capacity.note: The matrix argues for forward fab-labs at isolated sites with ad hoc demand rather than central production. Qualitative.

Speed.note: Times only: a noncritical part 'in as little as 45 minutes', and readiness gains where items 'cannot otherwise be procured'. Not valued.

tools.name: RAND Europe AM and obsolescence management in defence (PE-171), with Cranfield obsolescence-resolution cost metrics
tools.developer: RAND Europe (eds. Jon Freeman, Giacomo Persi Paoli). Contributors from armasuisse S+T, US Army ARDEC (G. Di Benedetto) and Cranfield University (J. Erkoyuncu, R. Roy, S. Williams, P. Colegrove, F. Martina, A. Busachi). Funded by armasuisse S+T.
tools.context: Defence obsolescence management for in-service equipment, with Swiss, UK and US perspectives (including Fleet Readiness Center East examples)
tools.processes: Generic AM, with DMLS 4340 steel data and WAAM (Cranfield)
tools.availability: Public RAND Perspective PE-171
tools.description: A collection of expert perspectives, not a model. The nearest decision elements are a 'window of opportunity' test for obsolescence, a list of resolution options (same component, form-fit-function replacement, emulation, redesign), and Cranfield cost metrics (Table 2) for choosing 'the most cost effective solution'. The cost metrics are not AM-specific.

NRE.note: Cranfield Table 2 quantifies non-recurring obsolescence-resolution costs by integration level, for example emulation from £52,100 (small) to £2.69m (very large). These are not AM-specific. The US Navy RESTORE 'SCAN to CAD to FAB' workflow is described without costs.

Production.note: Says small batches can be made 'on-demand at a constant cost' and that costs are 'largely predictable'. No unit figures.

QA_Qual.note: Requalification costs appear in the generic resolution-cost table. DMLS 4340 tensile data approach wrought properties. No AM qualification costing.

QA_Insp.note: Not addressed.

Storage.note: Proposes digital storage of designs instead of physical stock. The cost table includes existing stock (£300 per case). This is not an AM inventory model.

Shared_Capital.note: Not addressed.

Shared_Capacity.note: Mobile AM facilities are suggested for sustainment contracts. No pooling.

Speed.note: Anecdote: some FRCE repairs were made with AM 'over a few days' instead of three or more weeks. The window-of-opportunity concept is not valued.
