tools.name: NASA In-Space Manufacturing spares-logistics case (MSFC briefings citing Owens & de Weck 2016 and Cirillo et al. 2011)
tools.developer: NASA Marshall Space Flight Center In-Space Manufacturing (ISM) project (R. G. Clinton Jr.; T. Prater, N. Werkheiser, F. Ledbetter), citing analyses by Owens & de Weck (2016) and Cirillo et al. (2011)
tools.context: ISS and exploration missions: replacing pre-positioned corrective spares with on-orbit manufacturing and recycling
tools.processes: In-space polymer printing (Made In Space) demonstrated; in-space metal manufacturing still in technology maturation
tools.availability: Public NASA NTRS briefings. The underlying analyses were not opened.
tools.description: NASA's case for ISM rests on spares logistics. About 95% of corrective spares will never be used, and about 3,000 kg/yr of upmass compares with about 18,000 kg of ground spares ready to fly. Cited analyses report spares-mass cuts of 78.3% (ISM plus recycling) and 97.7% (the Owens & de Weck case). For a fluid-flow parts case, about one-third of components were assumed printable in space. No other NASA cost or part-selection tool was found besides NASA-STD-6030, which is scored elsewhere.

NRE.note: Only MSFC briefings were read and the underlying Owens & de Weck and Cirillo analyses were not opened; the briefings do not mention design or engineering effort.

Production.note: The briefings give no per-part cost for in-space manufacturing, and the underlying analyses, which were not opened, may or may not include cost.

QA_Qual.note: Briefings describe qualifying the metallurgical process on each AM machine, and list 'Verification & Certification Processes' as still under development. Not costed (NASA-STD-6030 is scored elsewhere).

QA_Insp.note: In-space NDE is listed as a gap. ISM specimens are inspected by structured-light scanning (±12.7 µm), CT, microscopy and mechanical tests. Not costed.

Storage.note: Cited analyses quantify spares-mass reduction (78.3%; 97.7%), motivated by ~95% of corrective spares never being used. Reported secondhand in NASA briefings.

Shared_Capital.note: The briefings do not address printer cost or sharing, and the underlying analyses were not opened.

Shared_Capacity.note: The briefings call the ISS Additive Manufacturing Facility a 'multi-user facility' but do not model capacity, and the underlying analyses were not opened.

Speed.note: The briefings report spares mass rather than time to part or availability, and the underlying analyses, which were not opened, may model availability.

tools.name: Braunberger AFIT MODA and metal L-PBF cost model for AM vs DLA procurement (C-130 parts)
tools.developer: 1st Lt Trever J. Braunberger, USAF, Air Force Institute of Technology (committee: Maj John Situ, Maj Ryan Kemnitz, Alfred E. Thal Jr.)
tools.context: USAF legacy aircraft parts with long lead times. Six C-130 troop-seat, rack and beam parts were judged not flight-safety critical. Selection criteria: price of $1,000 or more, lead time of 70 days or more, and a printable material.
tools.processes: Metal L-PBF/DMLS (EOS M290; Ti-6Al-4V)
tools.availability: Open thesis (DTIC AD1102526; AFIT Scholar etd/3748). The MODA is presented as a user tool; no software release is noted.
tools.description: A nine-criterion multi-objective decision analysis. Weights: quality 21.0%, lead time 20.1%, readiness 18.3%, price 14.6%, airworthiness 7.3%, expected life 6.3%, strength 6.2%, weight 4.8%, quantity 1.5%. Score bands: 86–100% is an 'extremely good candidate'; below 60%, use traditional methods. It is paired with an Atzeni & Salmi-based cost model and a guide to AM lab set-up costs ($1.94M for one metal lab). Single-part AM builds averaged $3,174.96 against $2,486.83 DLA prices, 27.6% more. Table 4.3 shows two of six parts cheaper with AM, while the text says three. AM lead times were 9–16 days against 71 to 120+ days.

NRE.note: Pre-processing cost CPRE = (ET x EC) + (TS x CO) includes an engineering-time term, and the thesis says NRE ('reengineering required to print a part, including creating digital 3D data, and programming') was included. Per-part pre-processing costs ($69-150, Table 4.3) exceed the $43.80 setup term, so engineering time is costed, although ET/EC values are not stated. Reverse engineering (150+ h) and parameter development (6+ months, $150k+) are listed but not allocated.

Production.note: Per-part material, pre-processing, processing (build-time formula, depreciation, energy, maintenance) and post-processing (labor $21.9/h, heat treatment $85/part). Results for six parts and for batch builds.

QA_Qual.note: Airworthiness is a MODA criterion (7.3% weight) and parameter-development testing costs are noted. Airworthiness approval is not costed and is called 'challenging and difficult'.

QA_Insp.note: Tensile test per build, with test-sample volume in material cost and $1,061 grips. Volumetric and NDI inspection are not included.

Storage.note: Notes that 'space does cost money', but storage and transport savings are called 'difficult to quantify' and are not modeled.

Shared_Capital.note: Depreciation of the ~$1.105M machine is charged per build hour (CDEP/MH, 8-year life). Multi-part builds are costed explicitly, cutting per-part cost by 33% (2 parachute racks) and 35% (3 bracket mounts) (Table 4.4). Sharing across sites or users is not modeled.

Shared_Capacity.note: Qualitative only: SME interviews call for a printer network and note distributed production 'may be cost effective' with more automation; no capacity pooling is modeled.

Speed.note: Lead time is compared per part (AM 9–16 days vs DLA 71 to 120+ days) and scored in the MODA alongside a separate readiness criterion. Time is quantified, not dollarized.

sources.title: Braunberger (2020) Providing Rational for Further Funding Additive Manufacturing Efforts in the Air Force, AFIT thesis (DTIC AD1102526)

tools.name: Crean AFIT metal AM per-part cost model and AM capability fielding costs
tools.developer: Capt Ryan C. Crean, USAF, Air Force Institute of Technology (advisor Alan W. Johnson)
tools.context: USAF long-lead-time parts: 10 NIINs, of which 7 were costed (PLT+ALT 324–611 days). Screening: unit cost over $1,000, ALT+PLT over 180 days, fits the EOS M290 envelope, not flight-critical. Also costs fielding three levels of AM capability.
tools.processes: Metal L-PBF/DMLS (EOS M290; titanium, aluminum, steel); production and desktop polymer printers for fielding costs
tools.availability: Open thesis (AFIT Scholar etd/791; core.ac.uk PDF)
tools.description: An Atzeni & Salmi-based cost model (material, pre-processing, processing, post-processing) with a layer-based build-time formula. It matched UDRI builds within 0–5.3%. Single builds averaged $3,144.74 per part and maximum batches $2,615.95. Before NRE, only 1 of 7 parts was cheaper with AM in single builds, and 3 with batching. Fielding one metal capability costs about $1.52–1.66M per alloy family.

NRE.note: Excluded from per-part cost, though the author says it 'will drive up the overall cost significantly'. Cites an AFLCMC estimate of '$1,000,000 to complete the NRE'. Build prep is $90 per build.

Production.note: Per part: material, depreciation (~$1.1M machine), maintenance ($18k/yr), energy, labor ($45/h) and heat treatment ($100). Cost shares are reported (machine 35%, post-processing 36%).

QA_Qual.note: Notes that AM process specifications do not yet exist, a barrier. Not costed.

QA_Insp.note: An ASTM E8 tensile coupon per build is costed at $300. Volumetric inspection is excluded. A CMM (~$100k) is listed.

Storage.note: Holding and transport savings are said to vary by part and location; not modeled.

Shared_Capital.note: Machine depreciation spread over machine-hours, batches of up to 16 parts per build, one machine per alloy family. No portfolio or user sharing.

Shared_Capacity.note: Pooling across sites is not modeled. A networked parts library is discussed qualitatively.

Speed.note: Current PLT+ALT is reported for each part (324–611 days), but AM lead time and readiness are not in the model.

tools.name: Daugherty & Heiple NPS USMC AM cost-benefit analysis (extrusion vs CLIP vs OEM supply)
tools.developer: Capt Zachary E. Daugherty and Capt Andrew J. Heiple, USMC (Naval Postgraduate School Acquisition Research Program, NPS-LM-18-018)
tools.context: USMC ground-equipment repair parts at 1st Maintenance Battalion, for example the AN/PVS-17c power knob, sold only in an assembly costing more than $4,000. Days-deadlined data come from MCBul 3000, GCSS and TLCM-OST.
tools.processes: Polymer only: material extrusion (Stratasys Fortus 250mc) and Carbon 3D CLIP. Not metal.
tools.availability: Open report (NPS DAIR)
tools.description: A cost-benefit analysis comparing OEM parts from the supply system with two AM options. It monetizes costs and the value of time (four valuation methods; Valuation 3 preferred) and compares NPVs in 2017 dollars. Sensitivity cases: baseline, time valuation, reduced days deadlined and equalized initial investment. AM has a production-level cost advantage, with CLIP ahead in 3 of 4 scenarios. Recommends a repository of printable files and continued Fortus use. The NPV tables were not in the text read.

NRE.note: Design and scanning examples are reported (4 h to design an NVG mount; a $25k scanner). Whether they enter the CBA was not verified.

Production.note: Production-level AM and OEM costs are monetized (material, initial investment), showing an AM cost advantage.

QA_Qual.note: Upgraded: the report discusses the parts approval process (slow organizational-level approval; MCSC and I&L vetting of fit, form and function) qualitatively; whether approval costs enter the CBA is not shown in the text read.

QA_Insp.note: Upgraded: the report describes testing printed parts for quality assurance (fit, form and function checks; a fan tested to standard) qualitatively; no inspection cost appears in the text read.

Storage.note: Stocking, transport and retrograde costs are discussed qualitatively, citing the Appleton report.

Shared_Capital.note: Initial investment is in the NPV, with an equalized-investment sensitivity case. No sharing across units.

Shared_Capacity.note: Recommends echeloning printers by maintenance level. Not modeled.

Speed.note: Days deadlined are valued in dollars (four valuation methods), included in NPV and tested in sensitivity cases.

tools.name: Holmström et al. rapid-manufacturing capacity-deployment alternatives for spare parts
tools.developer: Jan Holmström, Jouni Partanen, Jukka Tuomi, Manfred Walter
tools.context: Spare parts supply, illustrated with the aircraft industry
tools.processes: Rapid manufacturing (AM) generally
tools.availability: Journal of Manufacturing Technology Management 21(6):687–697. Paywalled; the abstract and two secondary descriptions were read.
tools.description: A conceptual comparison of centralized rapid-manufacturing (RM) deployment by OEMs with distributed deployment near the point of use by generalist service providers. One variant replaces regional distribution-center inventory with AM capacity. Distributed RM could improve service and cut inventory at the same time, but centralized OEM deployment is judged most feasible. RM spares supply is feasible only in particular situations because few parts can be made. Khajavi et al. (2018) note the authors did not use a case study to show which alternatives are feasible.

NRE.note: Only the abstract and secondary descriptions were read (full text paywalled); none mention design or engineering effort.

Production.note: Production cost is listed as a qualitative consideration (Abidar & Chaabane review table).

QA_Qual.note: Only the abstract and secondary descriptions were read; they do not mention qualification.

QA_Insp.note: Only the abstract and secondary descriptions were read; they do not mention inspection.

Storage.note: Inventory reduction and obsolescence are discussed qualitatively. Not quantified.

Shared_Capital.note: Khajavi et al. (2018) report that the authors judged decentralized deployment possible when AM machine utilization is high; qualitative.

Shared_Capacity.note: The core contribution is the alternative capacity-deployment configurations (central vs point of use). No model.

Speed.note: Better service from point-of-use deployment. Qualitative.

tools.name: Kunovjanek & Reiner AM diffusion and raw-material inventory model
tools.developer: Maximilian Kunovjanek, Gerald Reiner
tools.context: Raw-material supply chain under AM diffusion; the abstract names no case
tools.processes: Generic AM
tools.availability: International Journal of Production Research 58(5):1540–1554, DOI 10.1080/00207543.2019.1661537 (paywalled; abstract read)
tools.description: A dynamic evaluation model that uses the Bass diffusion model to estimate how AM adoption changes raw-material inventories. tools.name: Peron/Cantini qualification-cost model for AM vs conventional spare parts (Cantini et al. 2025)
tools.developer: Peron (NTNU), Cantini (Politecnico di Milano / Univ. Firenze), Coruzzolo and Lolli (Univ. Modena e Reggio Emilia), De Carlo (Univ. Firenze)
tools.context: Spare parts make-vs-buy between AM and conventional manufacturing, with qualification tests by criticality class (DNV-ST-B203 classes). Case: scale-model aircraft landing gear, DMLS vs high-pressure die casting.
tools.processes: Metal powder bed fusion (DMLS) vs high-pressure die casting
tools.availability: 2023 paper open access (IRIS UNIMORE); 2025 PPC paper abstract only
tools.description: Adds three qualification cost blocks to a production-cost comparison. Build process qualification is one-time for all classes (12 tensile, 3 impact, plus hardness, microstructure, porosity, chemistry and visual). Part qualification is one-time and C3 only, covering the full test set including surface and volumetric NDT and dimensional checks. Production testing is per build job: full set for C3, reduced for C2, negligible for C1. A CM batch shares one production test, while each AM build job needs its own. Test prices run from $10 (visual) to $150 (hardness or volumetric NDT), plus $20 per part for transport. Reported break-even quantity below which AM wins: 42 parts without qualification, 42 for C1, 8 for C2, 6 for C3. Sharing a build job among 4 parts raises the C3 break-even to 9. The 2025 extension embeds qualification costs in a spare-parts inventory cost model with holding and backorder costs (abstract only).

NRE.note: Models one-time CM tooling ($22,366) but not AM design-file/parameter NRE.

Production.note: Per-part production cost enters as inputs (AM $560.55/part; CM $22.68/part + tooling) taken from Atzeni & Salmi 2012, not computed from geometry/machine.

QA_Qual.note: One-time build-process and part qualification test sets priced by DNV criticality class.

QA_Insp.note: Per-build-job production testing priced by class, with batch-sharing rule and transport cost.

Storage.note: The 2023 paper has no inventory terms, and the 2025 abstract (full text not accessed) attributes holding costs to earlier models, so whether the extension models storage is not established.

Shared_Capital.note: Quantifies amortizing one-time qualification over part quantity (break-even N) and sharing tests across a build job; machine capital not modeled separately.

Shared_Capacity.note: Not addressed.

Speed.note: The 2023 paper does not value lead time, and the 2025 abstract attributes backorder costs to earlier models, so whether the extension values speed is not established.

tools.name: Verna et al. quality-inspection cost model for low-volume and AM production (2022)
tools.developer: Politecnico di Torino (Verna, Genta, Galetto, Franceschini)
tools.context: Choice of offline inspection strategy for low-volume production, with metal L-PBF case studies (AlSi10Mg).
tools.processes: Metal L-PBF/SLM (AlSi10Mg; EOS M290 in 2022 case)

tools.description: A probabilistic model per output characteristic covering defect probability p, false-alarm α, missed-defect β, inspection cost, necessary and unnecessary repair cost, and external failure cost. It yields D_tot (expected undetected defects) and C_tot (quality cost) to compare inspection strategies (2020). The 2022 paper adds quality costs to a per-part production cost model, with a return-on-inspection metric (ROII). In the L-PBF case, production cost was 18.56 €/part and quality-related costs were 14.40-31.69 €/part across three alternatives. In 2020, the most effective strategy cost about 4x the cheapest (€168.81 vs €42.36) with fewer undetected defects. CT was mentioned but not modeled.

NRE.note: Not addressed.

Production.note: 2022 model computes per-part material and manufacturing cost (powder, machine, operator, build/post-process times).

QA_Qual.note: Qualification not modeled.

QA_Insp.note: Per-part inspection cost traded against detection errors (α, β) and repair/escape costs; € results for L-PBF cases.

Storage.note: Not addressed.

Shared_Capital.note: Upgraded on opening the 2022 manuscript: the L-PBF system is charged at about 38 EUR/h from a 700 kEUR price depreciated over five years at 50% utilization (plus maintenance, rent and overheads), and job cost is divided by the 60 parts per job, so machine capital is amortized into per-part cost.

tools.developer: Direction generale de l'armement (DGA), France; defence AM working group launched early 2023
tools.context: French defence production and in-service support (MCO), including spares in theatre
tools.processes: All AM; metal named alongside polymers and ceramics; no specific metal process discussed
tools.availability: Public PDF (French)
tools.description: Policy note stating that AM complements rather than replaces conventional manufacturing, and that design offices should use AM where useful but not for every part. Its action plan covers defining MCO use cases and business models, a common agile qualification process, large machines serving the whole defence industry, and sharing demand forecasts with subcontractors. No scoring or cost method is given.

NRE.note: Not addressed beyond advising design offices to use AM where useful [1].

Production.note: States conventional methods will in some cases remain more suitable and cost-effective; no cost method [1].

QA_Qual.note: Calls for an agile, robust, generalisable qualification process with industry and a shared normative standard; not costed [1].

QA_Insp.note: Not addressed; post-processing appears only as a value-chain step [1].

Storage.note: Spares not held in stock and on-demand production near the point of use cited as benefits; not quantified [1].

Shared_Capital.note: Large French machines being developed to serve the whole defence industry, and consolidation of small firms; qualitative [1].

Shared_Capacity.note: Proposes a multi-sector network and sharing demand forecasts with subcontractors; no mechanism or model [1].

Speed.note: Cites Ukraine as showing AM's value for spares in theatre; expects lower MCO costs and operational constraints; not quantified [1].

tools.name: DGA OptiFab study: AM anti-blast protection and pre-qualified spare parts catalogue for light armoured vehicles
tools.developer: DGA (with the Agence de l'innovation de defense) and ARQUUS; testing at DGA Techniques aeronautiques, Toulouse
tools.context: French Army light armoured vehicles (VBL, PVP): workshop and overseas-operations (OPEX) spares
tools.processes: Not stated; composites and carbon fibre mentioned for protection parts
tools.availability: Described in trade press only
tools.description: DGA study that compares several manufacturing methods to pick the best for anti-blast parts. It also tests whether light-vehicle spares could be made additively in maintenance workshops. 'Cloned' AM parts are characterised against the originals, first on the bench and then on vehicles, toward a catalogue of pre-qualified spare parts.

Production.note: Only trade press describes the study; it gives no cost figures and does not show whether production cost is assessed.

QA_Qual.note: Cloned AM parts characterised against originals, then bench and vehicle tests, toward a pre-qualified catalogue; burden not quantified [1].

QA_Insp.note: Only trade press describes the study; it covers bench and vehicle characterisation but does not say whether per-part inspection is considered.

Storage.note: Reducing stockpiles named as a goal; not quantified [1].

Shared_Capital.note: Only trade press describes the study, and it does not say whether machine investment or sharing is assessed.

Shared_Capacity.note: Printers at certain bases, including overseas theatres; no counts or capacity model [1].

Speed.note: Parts made when needed without waiting for resupply; not quantified [1].

tools.name: ROK procedure for applying 3D-printed repair parts in operational units (DMSMS / FMECA / localisation screening with DT&E-OT&E qualification)
tools.developer: S. Yoo (ROK Ministry of National Defense), J. Hur (ROK Naval Academy), H. Lee (ROK Navy Force Support System Project Group)
tools.context: Weapon-system repair parts, Republic of Korea armed forces (2016-17 Army pilot; 2018 development plan of seven items; F-15K example)
tools.processes: PBF and DED named; processes used for the defence parts not stated; the 2016-17 Army pilot judged most metal parts unsuitable, mainly on strength
tools.availability: Open-access journal paper (Journal of Aerospace System Engineering 13(1), in Korean)
tools.description: Qualitative screening built on existing parts-localisation procedures. Candidates come from three pools: DMSMS-tracked obsolete parts, FMECA risk level 2-3 parts with poor MTBF/MKBF/MRBF, and foreign-sourced parts with high import-substitution value. Each passes DT&E, an installation test, OT&E and a military-suitability determination before being catalogued in a parts database. The programme (since 2017) was extended by a 2025 industry-defence ministry agreement.

NRE.note: The full paper mentions reverse modelling only as a software capability and does not treat design or reverse-engineering effort in its screening or qualification steps.

Production.note: Manufacturing ease and cost considered qualitatively for the localisation pool; cites an F-15K HPT cover plate at 90% lower purchase cost; no model [1].

QA_Qual.note: Staged DT&E, installation test, OT&E and military-suitability determination specified; burden not quantified [1].

QA_Insp.note: Refers to national quality guidelines covering equipment, materials, printed outputs and software; no per-part inspection cost [1].

Storage.note: Inventory effects not analysed [1].

Shared_Capital.note: The full paper calls for expanding military printing facilities and a national defence centre but does not address sharing machine investment.

Shared_Capacity.note: The full paper does not analyse sharing printing capacity between units or services.

Speed.note: FMECA/MTBF screening targets parts whose failures cut mission capability; cites procurement shortened by >30 days; not valued [1].

tools.name: Satair/Airbus AM spare-part pre-assessment and RapidSpares recertification route
tools.developer: Satair (Airbus aftermarket subsidiary) AM team with Airbus RapidSpares design offices; production at Airbus Filton Reference Manufacturing shop
tools.year: 2015-2020 (AM team since c. 2015; first certified metal flying spare 2020)
tools.context: Civil aircraft spares for the Airbus fleet: AOG and non-procurable parts
tools.processes: Titanium metal AM at a process-qualified shop (process not named in fetched sources); polymer parts also
tools.availability: Corporate practice; described only in press releases
tools.description: When a part becomes non-procurable or an AOG order arrives, Satair's AM team runs a short pre-assessment and hands candidates to Airbus RapidSpares design offices for redesign and recertification. In the A320ceo wingtip fence case, AM beat both re-tooling the casting and redesigning for machining. Satair reports more than 300 AM-certified part numbers.

NRE.note: Non-recurring cost compared across alternatives: mould replacement and machining redesign rejected, AM NRC 45% lower in one case. Method not published [1][2].

Production.note: A four-part shipset per 26 h build lowers cost per piece; no per-part cost model [1][2].

QA_Qual.note: Former cast part recertified in ~5 weeks via a new certification process; ships with EASA Form 1; shop process-qualified 2019. A case outcome, not a modelled burden [1][2].

QA_Insp.note: Only press releases describe the route; they mention post-processing but not inspection.

Storage.note: Only press releases describe the route, and they do not discuss inventory.

Shared_Capital.note: Only press releases describe the route, and they do not say whether machine investment is considered.

Shared_Capacity.note: Only press releases describe the route; they name the Filton print shop but say nothing about shared capacity.

Speed.note: AOG-triggered; total lead time reduced (no figure); a 2015 Qantas polymer part was prototyped within days; not valued [1][3].

tools.name: ST Engineering AM parts screening, business case and certification workflow (with EOS Additive Minds)
tools.developer: ST Engineering Aerospace (Advanced Manufacturing Design Centre, Singapore), with an EOS Additive Minds capability transfer
tools.context: Aircraft MRO and cabin interiors (passenger-to-freighter conversions) and obsolete parts, Singapore
tools.processes: Metal L-PBF/DMLS (EOS M 290 AlSi10Mg; SLM 280 IN625); SLS; FLM
tools.availability: Proprietary; described in a vendor-authored case study and company brochures
tools.description: A late-2018 capability-transfer programme gave ST Engineering a process for parts screening and selection, DfAM, business case analysis and critical-to-quality requirements. ST then built its own workflow covering DfAM, powder management, printing, inspection and post-processing. Parts are printed on demand from certified files under EASA/FAA/CAAS approvals, and more than 120 part numbers are in a production digital catalogue.

NRE.note: DfAM and assembly consolidation are part of the method; not costed [1].

Production.note: Business case analysis is a method step; no figures or model published [1][3].

QA_Qual.note: Qualification campaign to B-basis design values, proof-load tests, EASA STC/DOA/POA; burden not modelled in selection [1].

QA_Insp.note: Inspection is a workflow step and all parts undergo QA with traceability; not costed [1][3].

Storage.note: Virtual inventory; on-demand printing reduces non-moving inventory; not quantified [1].

Shared_Capital.note: Only a vendor case study and company brochures describe the method; it has a business-case step, but its contents, including machine investment, are not public.

Shared_Capacity.note: Certified files printed on qualified printers close to aircraft sites; no capacity model [1].

Speed.note: Shorter turnaround and 'drastically shorter lead time' claimed; no figures [1][3].

tools.name: Leonardo Aircraft Division AM spare-part candidate criteria (safety, feasibility, lead time >180 days, unscheduled removal rate band)
tools.developer: Leonardo S.p.A. Aircraft Division Customer Support (Caselle, Turin) with Politecnico di Torino (A. Pochettino MSc thesis; builds at IAM@PoliTo)
tools.context: Military aircraft spares and logistic support (C-27J, M-346, M-345), Italy
tools.processes: L-PBF (EOS M270) in AlSi10Mg and Ti6Al4V
tools.availability: Public MSc thesis
tools.description: Four screening criteria: non-safety-critical (binary); feasibility (geometry, material, volume, cost); procurement lead time over 180 days; and unscheduled removal rate of 0.050-0.500 per 1,000 flight hours. They yielded three use cases: a C-27J main landing gear bracket, an M-346 clevis and an M-345 connector. Leonardo reports more than 100 metal AM parts qualified and flying. This is separate from the earlier pass's Viano business-model entry for the same division.

NRE.note: CAD rebuilt from drawings and material substitution (Al 2024 to AlSi10Mg) discussed; effort not costed [1].

Production.note: Feasibility requires AM to be cost-effective at small to medium volumes; per-part AM costs for the three chosen parts (about EUR 69-105, from the AMOtool app) are estimated after selection, not within the screen.

QA_Qual.note: Safety-critical parts excluded; relies on Leonardo's existing certification path (AlSi10Mg certified); not quantified [1].

QA_Insp.note: Each order built in two copies, the second tested as first article (dimensional, chemical-physical, mechanical); not costed [1].

Storage.note: On-demand production to simplify warehouse management; not quantified [1].

Shared_Capital.note: The thesis lists the four criteria but says the full selection process is out of its scope, and its later chapters could not be extracted, so machine investment or sharing cannot be ruled out.

Shared_Capacity.note: The thesis says the full selection process is out of its scope and its later chapters could not be extracted, so whether capacity is considered is unconfirmed.

Speed.note: Quantified screening thresholds on lead time (>180 days) and removal rate, plus AOCP status; value of availability not modelled [1].

tools.name: EPRI Quick Insight Brief: Additive Manufacturing to Support Spare and Replacement Items (3002019767)
tools.developer: Electric Power Research Institute (EPRI)
tools.context: Power plant (incl. nuclear) spare and replacement items and obsolescence, US utilities
tools.processes: All seven AM process categories listed; worked examples are polymer (SLA, FDM) and ceramic, with no metal example
tools.availability: Free public download
tools.description: Short brief listing considerations for using AM for replacement items. They are process limits, QA scope (reverse-engineering measurements, CAD/CAM, fabrication), material equivalency for safety-related items, software control and counterfeiting. It gives utility examples and plans a member capability inventory, an application library and best-practice guidance.

NRE.note: QA must cover reverse-engineering measurements and CAD/CAM data creation; cost not separated [1].

Production.note: Example: AM connector ~$150 each with no minimum vs ~$120,000 OEM order with a 100-piece minimum per type; no cost model [1].

QA_Qual.note: Material equivalency must be established for safety-related items; best-practice guidance planned in 12-18 months [1].

QA_Insp.note: Verifying that items meet design named as a challenge; no inspection methods [1].

Storage.note: Avoiding minimum order quantities and managing obsolescence noted; no stocking guidance [1].

Shared_Capital.note: The brief notes the 'potential to share resources such as additive manufacturing and laser light measurement machines' among members and that one utility used an outside shop; no investment figures are given.

Shared_Capacity.note: Planned inventory of member and supplier AM capabilities that could lead to regional centres for spares [1].

Speed.note: Lead-time examples: OEM 46 weeks vs ~3 weeks AM; 3-month quote vs <1 week; not valued [1].

tools.name: EDF case-by-case AM of obsolete nuclear auxiliary-circuit parts and EDF Hydro WAAM programme
tools.developer: EDF (R&D, nuclear fleet and EDF Hydro) with partners incl. CIH, Institut de Soudure and INOVSYS
tools.context: Obsolete parts for French nuclear fleet auxiliary circuits and hydro units
tools.processes: L-PBF (SLM) for small parts; cold spray for tube repair; WAAM for hydro (e.g., ~1 m spherical-valve ring); printed moulds for casting
tools.availability: EDF web interviews; no published method
tools.description: EDF selects obsolete parts case by case and limits nuclear use to auxiliary circuits, not the primary circuit. Worn parts are 3D-scanned and rebuilt, either printed directly (a valve plug by SLM) or cast from a printed mould. The process is chosen by part size and use (SLM, cold spray or WAAM). EDF says it has not yet entered an industrial phase.

NRE.note: 3D scanning and rebuilding of worn parts described; not costed [1].

Production.note: Design and material optimisation said to reduce cost; no figures [1].

QA_Qual.note: RCC-M does not yet cover AM, and EDF aims to add it within three years; parts must match conventional mechanical performance [1].

QA_Insp.note: Adapting NDT (magnetic particle, ultrasonic, eddy current) to AM named as a main open question; not costed [1].

Storage.note: Only an EDF web interview describes the approach, and it does not discuss inventory.

Shared_Capital.note: Only an EDF web interview describes the approach, and it does not say whether machine investment or sharing is considered.

Shared_Capacity.note: Only an EDF web interview describes the approach; partners are named but their capacity is not discussed.

Speed.note: EDF Hydro aims to cut unit unavailability costs significantly, and cold spray shortens tube repairs; not quantified [1].

tools.name: Siemens Energy (Siemens Industrial Turbomachinery) Finspang AM burner repair and spares programme
tools.developer: Siemens Industrial Turbomachinery AB, Finspang (now Siemens Energy); Materials Solutions, Worcester (acquired 2016)
tools.context: Industrial gas turbine burner repair and spares, Sweden
tools.processes: L-PBF (EOS M270/M280, modified for burner-tip repair)
tools.availability: Corporate practice; trade press and Siemens software case material
tools.description: Problem-driven adoption: eroded burner tips are repaired by machining off the worn section and reprinting it, instead of buying new burners. QA_Qual.note: Repaired burners recertified; field evidence from inspection after 20,000 operating hours; not modelled [1].

QA_Insp.note: Automated 3D scanning and in-line/off-line monitoring planned; not costed [1].

Storage.note: On-demand printing of spares presented as a future goal; not quantified [1].

Shared_Capital.note: Trade press reports large investment in an eight-machine AM facility but does not say whether investment or sharing enters any part decision.

Shared_Capacity.note: Siemens AM Network links designers and service providers; not modelled [1].

Speed.note: Burner repair turnaround cut 70% (an outcome, not decision-model output) [1].

tools.name: GE annual part audit and per-part ROI screen for casting-to-AM conversion (LM9000 bleed air adapter caps)
tools.developer: GE Aviation (now GE Aerospace) with GE Additive; parts for Baker Hughes LM9000 turbines
tools.context: Aeroderivative land/marine gas turbine parts and spare-part sourcing, US
tools.processes: L-PBF (Concept Laser M2 Series 5), CoCr
tools.availability: Internal practice; one trade-press account
tools.description: In GE's 2020 annual part audit, the team reviewed hundreds of purchased castings, found 180 suitable for AM, and calculated ROI for each. It chose four CoCr bleed air adapter caps as the most profitable and checked them against quotes from four outside vendors. Reported results: ~35% lower manufacturing cost and 10 months from identification to prototypes.

QA_Qual.note: Printed parts matched cast quality within weeks; no formal qualification process described [1].

QA_Insp.note: Only one trade-press article describes the audit, and it does not say whether inspection cost enters the ROI.

Shared_Capital.note: Only one trade-press article describes the audit, and it does not say whether machine investment is in the ROI.

Shared_Capacity.note: Only one trade-press article describes the audit, and it does not mention capacity.

Speed.note: Time to market a stated criterion: 10 months vs a typical 12-18 for castings; spare-sourcing risk reduced; not valued [1].
